title: Urban Heat Islands
body: Urban neighborhoods can become warmer than nearby rural areas because asphalt and buildings absorb energy from sunlight and release heat slowly. This phenomenon is known as the urban heat island effect. Trees can reduce local temperatures by providing shade and releasing water vapor through their leaves. However, tree planting alone cannot solve every heat problem. The effect varies with building height, wind, available water, and the arrangement of green spaces. To evaluate a project, researchers compare temperature measurements from multiple locations and days rather than relying on a single afternoon reading. This approach helps separate a consistent cooling effect from ordinary changes in weather.

questions.question: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Cities should remove all paved streets
Urban heat has several causes and requires careful evaluation
Weather forecasts cannot predict city temperatures
Trees increase heat by absorbing water
questions.explanation: The passage explains the phenomenon, one mitigation strategy, and the need for repeated measurements.

questions.question: Why are measurements taken across multiple days?
options: To make the trees grow faster
To avoid confusing temporary weather with lasting effects
To measure only the warmest possible temperature
questions.explanation: Repeated measurements help distinguish a reliable cooling trend from day-to-day weather variability.

questions.question: What can be inferred about planting trees?
options: It is useful but its results depend on local conditions
It guarantees the same cooling in every city
It has no measurable effect on temperature
It works only in rural areas
questions.explanation: The writer notes shade and transpiration benefits but cautions that local conditions affect outcomes.

title: How Memory Changes with Retrieval
body: Students often reread notes because the activity feels familiar and efficient. Yet successfully recalling an idea without looking at the notes may provide a stronger opportunity for later remembering. Retrieval practice requires learners to reconstruct information, making gaps in their knowledge easier to identify. The effectiveness of this approach depends on the difficulty of the material, the spacing between attempts, and whether feedback is available. If students repeatedly practice an incorrect answer without correction, their confidence may grow while accuracy does not. For this reason, educators often pair low-stakes quizzes with prompt explanations and follow-up review. No single study method is ideal for every learner or subject, so an effective routine includes opportunities to adjust based on actual performance.

questions.question: Why can retrieval practice be useful?
options: It eliminates the need to understand ideas
It reveals what learners cannot yet recall
It prevents learners from making any mistakes
It works only when notes are visible
questions.explanation: The passage states that retrieving without notes makes knowledge gaps easier to identify.

questions.question: Which factor could make repeated quizzes less helpful?
options: Adjusting a study plan based on results
questions.explanation: Repeated uncorrected errors can increase confidence without improving accuracy.

questions.question: What does the author suggest about study methods?
options: Always reread for exactly an hour
Use one fixed method for every subject
Adapt the approach based on performance
questions.explanation: The concluding sentence recommends adjusting routines based on observable performance.

Their observations supported that prediction, although temperatures also depended on wind and building density. Instead of drawing a conclusion from one afternoon, they repeated the measurements over several weeks.

title: Learning and Evidence
body: Students often think rereading familiar material is the most efficient way to study. However, researchers have compared rereading with retrieval practice, which asks learners to recall information without looking at their notes. A learner may initially find retrieval difficult but later remember more. Results vary across subjects, so no one strategy should be treated as universally effective.

title: Wetlands and Flood Management
body: Wetlands can reduce flood risks by storing water when rainfall is unusually heavy. In a healthy wetland, soil, vegetation, and shallow pools slow the movement of water toward rivers. This does not mean wetlands prevent every flood. Their effectiveness depends on how much water the landscape can hold, the timing of a storm, and changes in nearby development. When towns replace wetlands with paved surfaces, rainwater may reach drainage systems more quickly. Some planners therefore combine wetland restoration with engineered barriers, rather than relying on either approach alone. To evaluate restoration projects, researchers compare flood levels across multiple storms and nearby areas with similar rainfall. Their findings may also reveal ecological benefits, such as habitat for insects and birds, but those benefits should be measured separately from flood protection.

questions.question: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Wetlands can reduce flood risks, but effectiveness depends on conditions
Bird populations are the only way to measure flooding
questions.explanation: The author describes storage benefits and limitations and recommends combined approaches.

questions.question: Why might paved surfaces increase flood pressure?
options: They absorb more water than soils
They accelerate movement of rainwater toward drains
questions.explanation: Water can reach drainage systems more quickly where land is paved.

questions.question: Why do researchers compare several storms?
options: To estimate effects beyond a single event
questions.explanation: Comparing storms reduces the chance of overinterpreting a single event.

questions.question: What can be inferred about ecological benefits?
options: They must be measured independently of flood outcomes
They prove flood protection is complete
They are identical to storm measurements
questions.explanation: The passage recommends separate measures for ecological and flood benefits.

title: Scientific Models and Prediction
body: A scientific model is a simplified representation of a complex system. Climate researchers, for example, use models to explore how temperature might change under different emissions scenarios. A model does not attempt to reproduce every feature of the real world. Instead, it focuses on relationships that are relevant to the question under study. Researchers test models by comparing predictions with observations, then revise assumptions when the comparison reveals consistent differences. Uncertainty remains because measurements are incomplete and because future human behavior cannot be known precisely. Communicating a range of possible outcomes is therefore often more responsible than announcing one exact number. Models are most useful when decision-makers understand both the conditions in which they perform well and the limitations of their assumptions. Different models can even reach different estimates while agreeing on a broad direction of change.

questions.question: Why do researchers simplify scientific systems?
options: To focus on relationships relevant to the question
questions.explanation: Models are simplified so they can represent the relevant mechanisms.

questions.question: How are models tested?
options: By replacing all measurements with opinions
By choosing a single perfect future
questions.explanation: Predictions are compared with observations; assumptions may then be revised.

questions.question: Why should a range of outcomes sometimes be reported?
options: Models always agree on one number
Future behavior and measurements create uncertainty
questions.explanation: The text notes incomplete measurement and unknowable future behavior.

questions.question: What is implied when different models agree on a direction?
options: They must have identical numerical predictions
Some broad conclusions may be shared despite different estimates
questions.explanation: Models can disagree on estimates while pointing toward a common trend.

title: Why Urban Trees Matter
body: Urban trees can lower surface temperatures by shading roads and buildings. Their leaves also release water vapor, which can cool nearby air. However, planting trees does not have the same effect everywhere. The amount of cooling depends on species, soil conditions, and access to water. A tree planted in a small paved area may struggle to grow, while the same species can thrive in a larger space with healthy soil. City planners therefore need to consider long-term maintenance rather than simply counting the number of newly planted trees.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Any tree will cool any city equally
Urban trees can reduce heat, but their impact depends on local conditions
Paved spaces are always better for tree growth
Tree planting should replace all road maintenance
questions.explanation: The passage explains benefits of shade and evaporation, then emphasizes differing local conditions and maintenance.

questions.question: Why might a tree in a paved area struggle?
options: Because city trees cannot release water vapor
Because the tree receives too much shade
Because limited soil space may restrict healthy growth
Because all urban soil is naturally too wet
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts a small paved area with a larger area of healthy soil, implying constrained growing conditions.

title: The Value of Replication
body: A single scientific study may report a striking result, but researchers often want to know whether the finding can be repeated. In replication, a different team carries out a comparable procedure to see whether a similar pattern emerges. Successful replication increases confidence, although it does not prove that an explanation is universally correct. A failed replication also requires careful interpretation: differences in participants, equipment, or circumstances may affect outcomes. For this reason, open methods and detailed reports help other teams evaluate what a result actually shows.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is one purpose of replication?
options: To guarantee that a theory is permanently correct
To find out whether a similar result appears in a comparable study
To replace every previous research finding
questions.explanation: Replication checks whether a comparable method produces a similar pattern, increasing confidence without guaranteeing truth.

questions.question: Why should an unsuccessful replication be interpreted carefully?
options: Researchers may use different participants or equipment
All results are random and uninformative
Open methods prevent researchers from comparing outcomes
questions.explanation: Differences in participants, equipment, or conditions can explain different outcomes, according to the passage.
